Fernando, Claire again. I have the debrief from the panel and I want you to hear it before we talk. They liked the numbers, and they said so twice. What they wrote down, and I am reading it to you, is that they never quite understood what you were actually hired to do in that group. Which surprised me, because you told me in five seconds. So here is what I want for the second round. Open with the mandate. One sentence. What the group asked you to deliver when you walked in, and what shape the finance function was in when you got there. Then the numbers. Not the other way round. And one more thing they flagged. When they asked what you would have done differently, you gave them a very careful answer and it sounded like you were protecting somebody. Give them a real one next time. Nobody trusts a CFO who has never changed his mind.

The honest answer is that I inherited a mess and I did not say so for eight months. My remit was to bring the reporting line under control, and the headcount I had was about a third of what the job needed. If I had asked for the backing in month one, I think I would have got it. I waited until I had the full picture, because that is how I am built, and by the time I asked, the year was gone and the board had stopped listening. With hindsight, that was the turning point of my whole tenure there, and I missed it. The lesson I took, and I have applied it since, is that you buy credibility by being early and wrong far more cheaply than by being late and right. If I could go back, that is the only thing I would change. Everything else I would do exactly the same way.
